name: Rome
summary: Founded by tradition in 753 BC on seven hills beside the Tiber, Rome grew from a cluster of hilltop villages into the capital of an empire that shaped Western law, language, engineering and government. As that empire faded it became the seat of the Roman Catholic Church, and across the Renaissance and Baroque it was remade again in travertine and marble. Uniquely among cities it surrounds a separate sovereign state, Vatican City, and still calls itself Caput Mundi — capital of the world.

events.title: The founding of Rome
events.body: Traditional founding of Rome by Romulus on the Palatine Hill.

events.title: Numa and the first religion
events.body: Numa Pompilius, the second king, is said to found Rome’s priesthoods and calendar.

events.title: The Republic is founded
events.body: The Romans expel the last king, Tarquin the Proud, and found the Republic.

events.title: The plebeians secede
events.body: The plebeians secede from the city, winning tribunes to defend their rights.

events.title: The Twelve Tables
events.body: The Twelve Tables set down Roman law in writing for the first time.

events.title: The Gauls sack Rome
events.body: A Gaulish army sacks the young city; only the Capitol holds out.

events.title: The Appian Way begins
events.body: Appius Claudius begins the Appian Way and Rome’s first aqueduct.

events.title: The Punic Wars
events.body: The Punic Wars against Carthage end with Rome master of the Mediterranean.

events.title: The murder of Tiberius Gracchus
events.body: The tribune Tiberius Gracchus is murdered over land reform — political violence enters the Republic.

events.title: The revolt of Spartacus
events.body: Spartacus leads a vast slave revolt before it is crushed.

events.title: Cicero and the Catiline plot
events.body: Cicero exposes and crushes the Catiline conspiracy to seize the state.

events.title: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
events.body: Caesar crosses the Rubicon, igniting civil war.

events.title: The Ides of March
events.body: Caesar is assassinated in the Senate on the Ides of March.

events.title: Augustus, first emperor
events.body: Octavian becomes Augustus, first emperor; the Republic gives way to Empire.

events.title: The Great Fire of Rome
events.body: The Great Fire of Rome burns for days; Nero blames the Christians.

events.title: The Colosseum opens
events.body: The Colosseum is inaugurated with a hundred days of games.

events.title: Hadrian's Pantheon
events.body: Hadrian rebuilds the Pantheon with its record-breaking concrete dome.

events.title: The Aurelian Walls
events.body: The Aurelian Walls rise around the city as barbarian pressure mounts.

events.title: Constantine at the Milvian Bridge
events.body: Constantine wins at the Milvian Bridge and turns the Empire toward Christianity.

events.title: Alaric's Visigoths sack Rome
events.body: Alaric’s Visigoths sack Rome — a shock that stuns the ancient world.

events.title: The Vandals sack Rome
events.body: The Vandals sack the city a second time.

events.title: The fall of the Western Empire
events.body: The last Western Roman emperor is deposed; antiquity gives way to the Middle Ages.

events.title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
events.body: Charlemagne is crowned emperor in St Peter’s on Christmas Day.

events.title: The Norman sack
events.body: Norman troops sack Rome while ostensibly rescuing the Pope.

events.title: The Papacy leaves for Avignon
events.body: The Papacy decamps to Avignon, leaving Rome impoverished and unruly.

events.title: Cola di Rienzo's republic
events.body: Cola di Rienzo seizes power dreaming of reviving the Roman Republic.

events.title: The new St Peter’s begins
events.body: Julius II lays the first stone of the new St Peter’s Basilica.

events.title: Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling
events.body: Michelangelo paints the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

events.title: The Sack of Rome, 1527
events.body: Mutinous troops of Charles V sack Rome, shattering the High Renaissance.

events.title: The plague of 1656
events.body: Plague sweeps through Rome, killing a large share of its people.

events.title: A short-lived Roman Republic
events.body: French revolutionaries proclaim a short-lived Roman Republic and depose the Pope.

events.title: Garibaldi defends Rome
events.body: Garibaldi and Mazzini defend a new Roman Republic before French troops restore the Pope.

events.title: The breach at Porta Pia
events.body: Italian troops breach the walls at Porta Pia; Rome joins a united Italy.

events.title: Capital of a united Italy
events.body: Rome becomes the capital of the Kingdom of Italy.

events.title: The March on Rome
events.body: Mussolini’s March on Rome brings the Fascists to power.

events.title: The Lateran Treaty and the Vatican
events.body: The Lateran Treaty creates the sovereign Vatican City.

events.title: Occupation and liberation
events.body: Rome is bombed, occupied by the Germans, and finally liberated in June 1944.

events.title: The Treaty of Rome
events.body: The Treaty of Rome founds what will become the European Union.

events.title: The 1960 Olympics
events.body: Rome hosts the Summer Olympic Games.

events.title: The Great Jubilee
events.body: The Great Jubilee draws tens of millions of pilgrims to the city.

places.name: Palatine Hill
places.note: Where tradition places Romulus’s founding of the city.

places.name: Roman Forum
places.note: The political and religious heart of the ancient city.

places.name: The Pantheon
places.note: Hadrian’s temple to all the gods; still the largest unreinforced concrete dome.

places.name: St Peter’s Basilica
places.note: Rebuilt 1506–1626 over the reputed tomb of St Peter, in Vatican City.

places.name: Trevi Fountain
places.note: Salvi’s Baroque fountain (1762), fed by the ancient Aqua Virgo.

unesco-91.title: Historic Centre of Rome — UNESCO World Heritage List

caveats: This timeline is compiled from general reference works — listed under Sources — rather than an event-by-event archive of primary documents, as the Mumbai timeline is. Treat it as a reliable outline, not a citation of record.
Dates for the earliest, legendary events are traditional rather than documented.

dynasties.note: Roman houses that shaped the city across its ages — Republican gentes, medieval barons and Baroque papal families.

list.name: The Julii (gens Julia)
list.summary: One of Rome’s oldest houses, claiming descent from Aeneas and the goddess Venus. It produced Julius Caesar and, by adoption, Augustus — founding the Julio-Claudian dynasty of emperors.

list.name: The Cornelii
list.summary: Among the most prolific noble houses, including the Scipiones — Scipio Africanus, who beat Hannibal at Zama — and the Gracchi on their mother’s side, who shook Rome with land reform.

list.legacy: Popes, cardinals and fortified family strongholds
list.name: The Colonna & Orsini
list.summary: Rival warrior families who fortified Rome’s ruins into castles and feuded for centuries over the city and the Papacy, each supplying popes and cardinals.

list.legacy: Bernini’s Rome — palaces, villas and fountains
list.name: The Barberini & Borghese
list.summary: Great houses that gave the Church popes (Urban VIII, Paul V) and spent that power reshaping Rome — commissioning Bernini, raising palaces and the villas that still ring the city. “What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did,” ran the jibe.
